title: Warming up
hook: psalms before the main prayer, to prepare the heart
tomorrow: Blessed is the one who spoke

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kaddish of the rabbis, for teachers and their students' students. Your line was pray for the teachers. Which teacher did you thank? That closes the morning blessings. Today, a new part of the prayer book. Day five hundred fifty-three.

No singer walks onstage cold. Backstage there are scales, humming, lip trills, the odd noises that loosen a voice. Runners jog before they run. Even a hard conversation goes better if you've had a minute to breathe in the car first. The body and the heart both need a ramp. The Jewish morning service has one built in. Before the Shema, before the standing prayer at its center, there's a long stretch of psalms and songs whose job, more or less, is to warm you up.
screen: `NO SINGER WALKS ON COLD.` → `THE HEART NEEDS A RAMP.` → `A STRETCH OF SONGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's called Pesukei d'Zimra, verses of song. It opens with a blessing, Baruch She'amar, closes with another, Yishtabach, and between them come psalms and passages of praise. Where does the idea come from? The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, remembers that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, to direct their hearts. The Talmud adds a principle from Rabbi Simlai: a person should always first set out the praise of God, and only then ask for anything. He learns it from Moses, who begins his plea to God with praise before he asks to enter the land. And in tractate Shabbat, Rabbi Yose says: may my portion be among those who complete the praise every day. The Talmud explains he meant these verses of song, the psalms near the end of the Book of Psalms. So the order is deliberate. Thanks for waking, then a little study, then song, and only then the central prayers. Praise before asking. Warmth before words of need. Some teachers love a play on the word zimra. The same three Hebrew letters can mean to sing and to prune, as you prune a vine. So the verses of song can be heard as verses of pruning: cutting away the distractions so the prayer can grow. That's wordplay, not the word's history, but some find it fits the experience.
screen: `PESUKEI D'ZIMRA: VERSES OF SONG.` · `AN HOUR TO DIRECT THE HEART.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN ASK.` · `TO SING, AND TO PRUNE.` · then, large: `WARM UP THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum before you pray, or before whatever comes next. Settle, and breathe. Close your mouth and let a low hum start in your chest. Any note. Feel it buzz in your ribs and your face. Let it rise and fall, like a slow tune with no words. If you know a melody from a prayer or a psalm, hum that. If not, hum anything gentle. Notice your breath lengthening and your shoulders softening. When the bell comes, you'll be warmed up. The bell holds the time.
Pesukei d'Zimra. Verses of song: the psalms and praise that warm the heart before the main prayer.

Your line: warm up the heart. A week of deeds without measure, learning first, the binding, what are we, words for offerings, a Kaddish for teachers, and verses of song. Today, before one hard task, take one minute to warm up. Day five hundred fifty-three.

screen: `DAY 553 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BLESSED IS THE ONE WHO SPOKE.`

howItsDone: Pesukei d'Zimra is said each morning between the morning blessings and the Shema, opening with Baruch She'amar and closing with Yishtabach; on Shabbat and festivals more psalms are added, and many communities sing parts of it aloud.

what it means: a deliberate warm-up. praise before asking, so the heart arrives ready.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (waiting an hour), Berakhot 32a (Rabbi Simlai, from Deuteronomy 3:23–24), and Shabbat 118b (Rabbi Yose's daily praise, read as the verses of song).

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'people find it true to the experience' softened to 'some find it fits the experience'. Otherwise unchanged.
Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (chasidim harishonim waited an hour); confirm.
Berakhot 32a: Rabbi Simlai, praise before petition, derived from Moses in Deuteronomy 3:23–25; confirm.
Shabbat 118b: Rabbi Yose, 'may my portion be among those who complete Hallel every day', explained as pesukei d'zimra; confirm.
zamar = sing / prune (Leviticus 25:3): presented explicitly as wordplay, not etymology. Confirm acceptable.
